name: sill
problem_statement: Dragging work between apps means losing context — files pile in Downloads, clipboard gets overwritten, and temporary staging areas don't exist on Mac. Creatives and builders need a beautiful, persistent shelf to park fragments while they work.
thesis: Yoink and Dropzone proved the market for drag-and-drop staging, but they're utilitarian eyesores. There's a gap for a craft-first shelf app with the polish of Things 3 — spatial, visual, and alive. The decay mechanic (items fade after 7 days untouched) is a novel twist that keeps the shelf from becoming another junk drawer.
differentiation: Items decay — the shelf is alive, not a static junk drawer, and the material design language (warm wood grain, not generic blur) makes it feel like furniture on your desktop.
target_user: Quinn primary, designers and developers who work across 5+ apps daily
initial_brief: Build a menubar app that drops down a translucent shelf — a horizontal strip with rounded slots. Users drag files, text snippets, images, and URLs onto the shelf from any app. Items sit there persistently across restarts. Each item shows a tiny preview (thumbnail, text excerpt, favicon). Items can be dragged back out into any app. The first iteration should nail the core interaction: drop-on, preview, drag-off. Use a warm, tactile material aesthetic — think wooden windowsill, not frosted glass. No settings screen yet, no preferences — just the shelf and the interaction. 8 slots max. Items older than 7 days begin to visually fade (opacity drops) as a gentle nudge to clear or use them.
pick_justification: Sill wins because the core interaction (drag-on, preview, drag-off) can be polished to gem-quality in 30 days, the market is proven but the incumbents are ugly, and the decay mechanic gives it genuine novelty. Compost is philosophically richer but risks scope creep; Ember requires Accessibility API permissions that create friction at install.

candidates_considered.name: compost
candidates_considered.thesis: Every note app assumes you're writing something coherent. Compost celebrates incompleteness — it's a drop zone for creative scraps that surfaces unexpected connections between fragments over time using on-device embeddings. The composting metaphor is the product: raw material decomposes into fertile ideas.

candidates_considered.name: ember
candidates_considered.thesis: Screen Time and RescueTime track duration. Ember tracks creative coherence — sustained focus in one context vs. frantic app-switching. The visualization is a living ember in the menubar that glows brighter during flow and dims during scatter. It's a biofeedback loop for creative work, not a guilt machine.
